title: The hug at the wedding
hook: Your uncle insists on a hug. Everyone's watching.

n1.text:
It's your cousin Riya's sangeet. The hall is loud, the aunties are in a row of gold chairs, and your mom is steering you by the elbow towards Suresh uncle. Dad's cousin. You've met him maybe twice.
Suresh uncle: Arre! Itne bade ho gaye! Come, give your uncle a hug.
His arms are already open. The aunties are watching.

choices.label: Hug him anyway
choices.consequence: It's over in three seconds. His hand stays on your back a little longer than you'd like. Everyone smiles. You feel that small sour feeling you already know.
choices.expert_note: Going along to keep the peace is something almost everyone does. It doesn't mean you wanted it. Noticing that sour feeling is where a boundary starts.

choices.label: Fold your hands: "Namaste, uncle!"
choices.consequence: You smile, fold your hands and take half a step back. He pauses, then laughs a bit too loudly. "Bahut formal ho gaye!" One aunty raises an eyebrow. Nobody dies.
choices.expert_note: A different greeting is a complete answer. You showed respect without handing over your body. Awkward is not the same as rude.

choices.label: Pretend your phone is ringing
choices.consequence: You hold up your phone, mouth "one second" and walk off. It works. From across the hall you can see him, and you know this comes back at dinner.
choices.expert_note: Getting out is a valid move when you need one. It just doesn't tell anyone where the line is, so the moment tends to come round again.

n2.text:
Near the buffet, your mom pulls you to one side.
Mom: Why are you being so stiff with Suresh uncle? He's family. Log kya kahenge.

choices.label: "Sorry. I'll be nicer."
choices.consequence: Mom relaxes straight away and hands you a plate. The evening goes smoothly. You spend it rehearsing what you wish you'd said.
choices.expert_note: Apologising for a boundary quietly teaches you it was wrong to have one. Keeping the peace tonight is okay. It's worth noticing what it cost.

choices.label: "I'm not being rude. I just don't like hugging people I barely know."
choices.consequence: Mom sighs. "In our time nobody asked us." But she doesn't push. Later you catch her watching you, thinking.
choices.expert_note: Calm, about your own feeling, and no accusation in it. Parents rarely agree on the spot. Hearing it said plainly is often the first time they consider it at all.

choices.label: "He makes me uncomfortable, Mom."
choices.consequence: Mom goes quiet. "Did he do something?" You say no, it's just a feeling. She looks at you for a second. "Stay near me then."
choices.expert_note: You don't need proof to feel uncomfortable. Telling one adult you trust changes who is looking out for you in that room.

n3.text: End of the night. Everyone is doing goodbyes at the door. Suresh uncle is walking towards you and his arms are opening again. Mom is standing next to you.

choices.label: Step forward with a namaste: "Good night, uncle. Safe drive."
choices.consequence: You get there first, hands folded, voice warm. He stops, and folds his hands back, a little stiffly.
choices.expert_note: Going first lets you set the greeting instead of reacting to his. Warm words and a clear body can go together.

choices.label: Let it happen. It's one more hug.
choices.consequence: It's quick. Nothing terrible happens. You hold your breath through it.
choices.expert_note: Choosing not to fight this one, tonight, is also a choice. It doesn't use up your right to choose differently next time.

choices.label: Glance at Mom
choices.consequence: Mom sees your face. Her hand lands on your back. "Chalo chalo, we're getting late!" and she is already moving you towards the car.
choices.expert_note: Asking for backup, even with a look, is not weakness. Most boundaries hold better with one more person behind them.

end_a.title: The namaste holds
end_a.text: In the car, Dad says you've become "too modern". Mom says nothing. You feel shaky, and also a little taller than you did this morning.
end_a.takeaway: Your body, your call, even with family. A respectful no is still respectful.

end_b.title: One more hug
end_b.text: On the ride home you think about the next wedding, in December, and realise you'd like to have a plan by then.
end_b.takeaway: Going along once doesn't cancel your right to say no next time.

end_c.title: Mom moves first
end_c.text: She never brings it up again. You're not sure she really understood. But she moved.
end_c.takeaway: You don't have to hold a boundary alone. One person in your corner changes the room.
